title: Delete Columns to Make Sorted II
statement:
You are given `strs`, a list of `n` strings that all have the same length. Picture them stacked as rows of a grid, so position `j` of every string forms column `j`. You may delete any set of columns; a deleted column loses its character in every string, and the remaining characters keep their order.

After deleting, the strings must be in non-decreasing lexicographic order (`strs[0] <= strs[1] <= ... <= strs[n - 1]`). Return the fewest columns you need to delete to achieve this. The characters inside a single string do not need to be sorted; deleting every column leaves only empty strings, which always count as ordered.
constraints: All strings in strs have the same length
strs[i] contains only lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

Trying every set of columns costs O(2^w). Instead walk the columns from left to right and decide each one greedily. Keeping a column is always at least as good as deleting it, **as long as it does not break the order** of any adjacent pair that is still tied. Once a kept column puts `strs[i]` strictly before `strs[i + 1]`, that pair is settled forever: later columns can never reorder it. So the only pairs that matter for a column are the ones still tied on everything kept so far.

## Approach

1. `decided[i]` is true once the kept columns already make `strs[i] < strs[i + 1]`.
2. For each column `col`, check every adjacent pair that is not yet `decided`. If any has `strs[i][col] > strs[i + 1][col]`, keeping the column would break the order.
3. If so, delete it: add one to `deletions` and move on without changing `decided`.
4. Otherwise keep it, and mark every pair with `strs[i][col] < strs[i + 1][col]` as `decided`.
5. Return `deletions`.

## Example 1, step by step

`strs = ["ca", "bb", "ac"]`, nothing decided yet. Column 0 holds `c, b, a`; the pair (0, 1) has `c > b`, so the column is deleted and `deletions = 1`. Column 1 holds `a, b, c`; no undecided pair goes down, so it is kept and both pairs become decided. The answer is `1`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n · w): each column scans the adjacent pairs at most twice.
- Space: O(n) for `decided`.

## Pitfalls

- Pairs already settled by an earlier kept column must be ignored; otherwise a harmless column like the last one in Example 2 gets deleted.
- Only mark pairs as decided for columns you keep; a deleted column must not settle anything.
- Equal characters leave a pair undecided, so later columns still have to respect it.
- The strings' own letters need not be sorted; only the order between rows matters.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | number of strings |
| `width` | length of every string (number of columns) |
| `decided` | `decided[i]`: kept columns already put `strs[i]` strictly before `strs[i + 1]` |
| `deletions` | columns deleted so far |
| `col` | current column |
| `keep` | whether the current column can stay without breaking the order |
